Act two. Before we build anything: what tracing already gives us, and where it stops.

Source: Ch 14

KASPER

Two words for the rest of the talk.

On the left, one span: the record of one step, like one tool call. It has a name, a start, an end, and labels: facts about the work.

On the right, a trace: every span that shares one trace id. Each span points at its parent, so they form a tree. Read it top down: the customer submits, the agent runs, calls a tool, and the gateway asks the policy service. One request, one story.

Source: Ch 3

KASPER

That tree only holds together if every span carries the same trace id.

Think of a parcel with a tracking number. Every depot scans the label. On the left, every hop kept the label on: one story. On the right, one hop stuck on a new label, and the history splits in two. Nothing errors. You just can't follow it any more.

And agents add a lot of new hops.

Source: Ch 3

KASPER

This is the label: the W3C traceparent header. Version, always zero zero. The trace id, the tracking number, the same on every span. The parent id, replaced at every hop, like a depot stamp. The flags: zero one means sampled.

The news: since the July twenty-eighth MCP spec, SEP-414 puts the same label inside the message, in params underscore meta. So context survives transports with no headers, like stdio. Northstar sends both copies. The gateway reads only the header.

KASPER

Thanks, William. Everything I'll show you is OpenTelemetry, so one minute on what that is.

Two words first. A span is the record of one step, like one tool call. A trace is every span of one run, held together by one trace id that every hop passes on, through MCP and A2A too. Drop it at one hop and the story falls apart.

On the left: OpenTelemetry is the standard every service in the demo speaks. Traces, metrics and logs, from one SDK per service, into one Collector, which fans out to whatever backend you like: Jaeger, OpenSearch, Prometheus here. And it gives everyone shared names, the semantic conventions: http-dot-something for web calls, gen_ai-dot-something for model and agent calls: which model, how many tokens, which tool, and, if you opt in, the prompts and answers themselves.

On the right: the names that are ours. A policy decision, a human review, an autonomy level: no convention covers those. So we write them down in Weaver, OpenTelemetry's own tool for this. Define them in YAML, on top of the official conventions. Check the registry in CI. Generate the docs from it. And live-check: the Collector sends Weaver a copy of everything the cluster really emits, and it fails if we emit a name we never defined.

Telemetry names are an API. Weaver checks the API against what really runs.

Source: telemetry/registry (manifest.yaml: northstar on semantic-conventions v1.44.0; policy.yaml northstar.policy.decision); scripts/check-registry.sh (otel/weaver v0.28.0: registry check, registry generate markdown); deploy/observability/weaver-live-check.yaml and telemetry/live-check.toml (fail_on = violation)

KASPER

So what can the gen_ai names answer? Read across: one, a question an investigator asks; two, the attribute that answers it; three, dimmed rows are the content.

The dark rows are the spec's defaults: kind of step, model, act or stop, tool, conversation.

The dimmed rows are content: what it was told, what it decided, what it asked for, what happened. The most sensitive data, so the spec makes them opt-in. Many libraries capture them anyway: at their defaults, four of seven wrote the model's output. And exactly what an auditor needs. Hold that until after the demo.
